title: If Kindergarten were like Social Media Marketing: satire of social media tactics
summary: A satirical essay that applies social media marketing rules to kindergarten to expose their absurdity. It implicitly critiques forced authenticity, content-formula thinking, daily posting for top-of-mind, how-to eBooks from the already-popular, transactional compliments, and monetizing attention too early. Mostly humor with little direct actionable advice.

principles.text: Forced 'authenticity' backfires: radical honesty isn't rewarded the way marketers promise.
principles.quote: After a stern lecture on the value of being authentic, little Richard Neuman courageously admits that during recess he pooed his pants and buried the evidence in the gravel under the blue slide. His bravery is not met with the loving acceptance the teacher had promised.

principles.text: Advice from the already-popular doesn't transfer; knowing the tactics doesn't give you their audience.
principles.quote: It's well received from pre-K through third grade, but although it contains clear examples and actionable advice, somehow the unpopular kids still never get invited to the cool kids' slumber parties.

principles.text: Transactional flattery to build relationships reads as insincere and damages reputation.
principles.quote: Learning that making nice comments about people helps forge relationships, little Bobby Gray compliments the entire kickball team. He is denied the coveted spot and earns the nickname "Bobby Bootlicker."

principles.text: Mechanically posting daily to 'stay top-of-mind' is a questionable tactic that devalues the work itself.
principles.quote: Children are encouraged to make at least one drawing or painting every day. Refrigerator art goes stale quickly and you want to stay top-of-mind with your parents.
